## Overview

This exercise follows [Chapter 18: Market Area Analysis for Retail and Service Locations using Huff model](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap18). It uses Taichung's village boundaries, store locations, 2019 population and the supplied sales records. The classroom extension is a map of store trade areas, with a categorical field named `TA`, as shown in the reference photographs.

I calculate a probability of choosing each listed store from each village. I then make two different maps: a probability map for store BT, and a dominant-store map that assigns each village to its highest-probability store. The second map summarises the probabilities; it does not imply that everyone in a village visits the same store.

The questions are which villages are more strongly associated with BT, which store has the largest modelled probability in each village, and how the population-weighted store allocations relate to recorded sales.

## Getting started

The chapter's packages are attached in one `pacman::p_load()` call. `knitr` supplies readable result tables and `ragg` draws PNG figures without an X11 dependency. The file check stops execution if the course inputs are absent; it does not replace them with simulated data.

```{r}
#| label: setup

if (!requireNamespace("pacman", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pacman", repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
}
pacman::p_load(sf, tidyverse, MCI, tmap, ggstatsplot, knitr, ragg)

options(scipen = 999)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png")
tmap_mode("plot")
source("scripts/trade_areas.R")

required_files <- c(
  unlist(lapply(c("STORES_TC", "TOWN_TC", "VILLAGE_TC"), function(layer) {
    file.path("data", "geospatial", paste0(layer, c(".shp", ".shx", ".dbf", ".prj")))
  })),
  file.path("data", "aspatial", c("pop2019.csv", "Store_sales_data.csv", "storeCD.csv"))
)
missing_files <- required_files[!file.exists(required_files)]
if (length(missing_files)) {
  stop(paste("The actual course inputs are required. Missing files:",
             paste(missing_files, collapse = "\n"), sep = "\n"))
}
dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
fmt <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE, scientific = FALSE)
```

## Importing and checking the data

The inputs are the course files supplied for this exercise, documented in the [data record](data/README.md). The original 28-store `STORES_TC` layer is used throughout. The separate `STORES_TC1` layer includes an additional store, NS, and is not mixed into this baseline analysis. Restore the local inputs with `Rscript scripts/import_data.R /path/to/course/data` before rendering a fresh checkout.

I use `st_read()` for the three spatial layers and `read_csv()` for the two tables. The chapter's executable code uses the `_TC` layers, including `TOWN_TC`, even though its opening list mentions `_TN`. I follow the Taichung code and use TWD97 / TM2 zone 121, EPSG 3826, so planar distances are measured in metres.

```{r}
#| label: import-data

stores_raw <- st_read("data/geospatial", "STORES_TC", quiet = TRUE)
town_raw <- st_read("data/geospatial", "TOWN_TC", quiet = TRUE)
village_raw <- st_read("data/geospatial", "VILLAGE_TC", quiet = TRUE)
stopifnot(
  !is.na(st_crs(stores_raw)), !is.na(st_crs(town_raw)),
  !is.na(st_crs(village_raw))
)
invalid_before <- c(
  Stores = sum(!st_is_valid(stores_raw)), Towns = sum(!st_is_valid(town_raw)),
  Villages = sum(!st_is_valid(village_raw))
)
stores <- stores_raw |> st_make_valid() |> st_transform(3826)
town <- town_raw |> st_make_valid() |> st_transform(3826)
village_raw <- village_raw |> st_make_valid() |> st_transform(3826)

pop2019_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/aspatial/pop2019.csv", show_col_types = FALSE,
  col_types = cols(V_ID = col_character(), .default = col_guess())
)
store_sales <- read_csv(
  "data/aspatial/Store_sales_data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE, na = "",
  col_types = cols(`Store Code` = col_character(), .default = col_guess())
)
store_codes <- read_csv("data/aspatial/storeCD.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
stopifnot(
  nrow(problems(pop2019_raw)) == 0, nrow(problems(store_sales)) == 0,
  !anyDuplicated(stores$Store_CD), !anyDuplicated(village_raw$VILLCODE),
  !anyNA(stores$Store_CD), !anyNA(village_raw$VILLCODE),
  !anyDuplicated(store_codes$Store_CD),
  setequal(store_codes$Store_CD, stores$Store_CD),
  all(st_is_valid(stores)), all(st_is_valid(town)),
  all(st_is_valid(village_raw)),
  all(c(st_crs(stores)$epsg, st_crs(town)$epsg,
        st_crs(village_raw)$epsg) == 3826)
)
input_counts <- tibble(
  Input = c("Stores", "Town boundaries", "Village boundaries",
            "Population rows", "Sales rows"),
  Observed = c(nrow(stores), nrow(town), nrow(village_raw),
               nrow(pop2019_raw), nrow(store_sales)),
  Chapter_reference = c(28, 28, 622, 625, 5499)
)
kable(input_counts, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
      caption = "Observed counts alongside the chapter's reference counts")
```

The geometry checks required `r sum(invalid_before)` repairs in memory. The original files are left unchanged. The chapter's counts are a reference for checking the supplied version, not values used to fill gaps in the data.

## Preparing the tables and joins

### Aggregating recorded sales by store

I sum bills and amounts by `Store Code`, then use a named `left_join()` to attach the totals to the store layer. Every store receives `Store_size = 100`, matching the chapter. This is assumed equal attractiveness, not a measured shop-floor area. Sales are held aside for comparison rather than being used to define attractiveness and then claimed as independent validation.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-store-sales

stopifnot(
  !anyNA(store_sales$`Store Code`),
  all(is.finite(store_sales$Bills)), all(is.finite(store_sales$Amount)),
  all(store_sales$Bills >= 0), all(store_sales$Amount >= 0)
)
store_sales_aggre <- store_sales |>
  group_by(`Store Code`) |>
  summarise(Total_Bill = sum(Bills), Total_Sales = sum(Amount), .groups = "drop")
sales_without_location <- store_sales_aggre |>
  anti_join(st_drop_geometry(stores), by = join_by(`Store Code` == Store_CD))
stores <- stores |>
  left_join(store_sales_aggre, by = join_by(Store_CD == `Store Code`),
            relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  mutate(Store_size = 100) |>
  arrange(Store_CD)
stopifnot(!anyNA(stores$Total_Sales), all(stores$Store_size > 0))
kable(st_drop_geometry(stores) |>
        select(Store_CD, Total_Bill, Total_Sales, Store_size),
      format.args = list(big.mark = ","), caption = "Recorded sales for the mapped stores")
```

There are `r nrow(sales_without_location)` additional sales-table code categories without a location in the supplied store layer. They are listed separately in the audit output and are not silently treated as mapped competitors. The reader uses `na = ""` to preserve the literal code text `NA` in `r sum(store_sales[["Store Code"]] == "NA")` rows; its meaning is not inferred or used to create a new mapped store.

### Matching population to villages

`V_ID` contains a hyphen, while `VILLCODE` does not. I remove that separator, preserve both IDs as text, check uniqueness, and join explicitly. An unmatched village is not assumed to have zero population. Following the chapter, it is excluded from the model, but remains visible as grey map context.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-population

pop2019 <- pop2019_raw |>
  mutate(V_ID = str_remove_all(V_ID, "-"))
stopifnot(!anyNA(pop2019$V_ID), !anyDuplicated(pop2019$V_ID))
village_joined <- village_raw |>
  left_join(pop2019, by = join_by(VILLCODE == V_ID), relationship = "one-to-one")
excluded_villages <- village_joined |>
  filter(is.na(P_CNT)) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(VILLCODE, TOWNNAME, VILLNAME)
unmatched_population <- pop2019 |>
  anti_join(st_drop_geometry(village_raw), by = join_by(V_ID == VILLCODE))
village <- village_joined |>
  filter(!is.na(P_CNT)) |>
  arrange(VILLCODE)
stopifnot(
  nrow(village_joined) == nrow(village_raw), nrow(village) > 0,
  !anyNA(select(st_drop_geometry(village), H_CNT, P_CNT, M_CNT, F_CNT)),
  all(village$P_CNT > 0), all(village$H_CNT > 0),
  all(village$M_CNT >= 0), all(village$F_CNT >= 0),
  all(village$M_CNT + village$F_CNT == village$P_CNT)
)
kable(tibble(
  Check = c("Villages with matched population", "Unmatched village polygons",
            "Population rows without a matching polygon", "Modelled population"),
  Result = c(nrow(village), nrow(excluded_villages),
             nrow(unmatched_population), sum(village$P_CNT))
), format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
if (nrow(excluded_villages)) {
  kable(excluded_villages, caption = "Excluded polygons: population was not matched")
}
```

## Computing the distance and interaction matrices

The chapter calls `st_point_on_surface()`. That returns a point inside each polygon; it is not necessarily its geometric centroid. I use the same method, then calculate straight-line distances to all stores with `st_distance()`. These are not road-network distances or travel times.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-interaction-matrix

village_center <- st_point_on_surface(village)
distmat <- st_distance(village_center, stores)
rownames(distmat) <- village$VILLCODE
colnames(distmat) <- stores$Store_CD
distmat_numeric <- matrix(as.numeric(distmat), nrow = nrow(village),
                          dimnames = dimnames(distmat))
stopifnot(
  all(is.finite(distmat_numeric)), all(distmat_numeric > 0),
  identical(rownames(distmat_numeric), village$VILLCODE),
  identical(colnames(distmat_numeric), stores$Store_CD)
)
distmat_long <- as.data.frame(distmat_numeric) |>
  rownames_to_column("VILLCODE") |>
  pivot_longer(-VILLCODE, names_to = "Store_CD", values_to = "distance")
interaction_matrix <- distmat_long |>
  left_join(st_drop_geometry(stores) |> select(Store_CD, Store_size),
            by = "Store_CD", relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  select(VILLCODE, Store_CD, Store_size, distance) |>
  as.data.frame()
stopifnot(
  nrow(interaction_matrix) == nrow(village) * nrow(stores),
  !anyDuplicated(interaction_matrix[c("VILLCODE", "Store_CD")]),
  !anyNA(interaction_matrix)
)
kable(tibble(
  Origins = nrow(village), Destinations = nrow(stores),
  Pairs = nrow(interaction_matrix),
  Minimum_metres = min(interaction_matrix$distance),
  Median_metres = median(interaction_matrix$distance),
  Maximum_metres = max(interaction_matrix$distance)
), digits = 1, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

Zero distances would make inverse-distance weights undefined. The check above stops rather than quietly substituting an arbitrary minimum distance.

## Computing Huff probabilities

For village $i$ and store $j$, the chapter's default power model is

$$p_{ij}=\frac{A_j^\gamma d_{ij}^{\lambda}}
{\sum_k A_k^\gamma d_{ik}^{\lambda}},\qquad \gamma=1,\quad\lambda=-2.$$

A store's contribution increases with attractiveness and decreases with distance. The denominator compares that contribution with all listed competitors. I make the package defaults explicit and verify the output against the formula. The probabilities for each village must sum to one.

```{r}
#| label: compute-huff-model

huff_share <- huff.shares(
  interaction_matrix, "VILLCODE", "Store_CD", "Store_size", "distance",
  gamma = 1, lambda = -2, atype = "pow", dtype = "pow"
)
huff_share <- as_tibble(huff_share) |>
  mutate(p_ij = as.numeric(p_ij))
formula_check <- huff_share |>
  mutate(direct_weight = Store_size * distance^(-2)) |>
  group_by(VILLCODE) |>
  mutate(direct_probability = direct_weight / sum(direct_weight)) |>
  ungroup()
probability_checks <- huff_share |>
  group_by(VILLCODE) |>
  summarise(Stores = n(), Probability_sum = sum(p_ij), .groups = "drop")
formula_error <- max(abs(formula_check$p_ij - formula_check$direct_probability))
stopifnot(
  nrow(huff_share) == nrow(interaction_matrix),
  all(is.finite(huff_share$p_ij)), all(huff_share$p_ij >= 0 & huff_share$p_ij <= 1),
  all(probability_checks$Stores == nrow(stores)),
  max(abs(probability_checks$Probability_sum - 1)) < 1e-10,
  formula_error < 1e-10
)
kable(tibble(
  Check = c("Largest probability-sum error", "Largest direct-formula difference"),
  Difference = c(max(abs(probability_checks$Probability_sum - 1)), formula_error)
), digits = 12)
```

These parameters are assumptions from the teaching example, not fitted consumer preferences. With all stores assigned attractiveness 100, that constant cancels from the probability formula. The result is driven by relative distance to the listed stores.

## Trade area for store BT

The chapter's code selects BT, although one sentence mentions TG. I consistently use BT. The legend is outside the map, and darker blue indicates a larger modelled patronage probability.

```{r}
#| label: map-bt-probability
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 12
#| fig-cap: "Huff patronage probability for BT; grey polygons have no matched population and are excluded"

stopifnot("BT" %in% stores$Store_CD)
market_share <- huff_share |>
  filter(Store_CD == "BT") |>
  select(VILLCODE, p_ij)
Trade_area <- village |>
  left_join(market_share, by = "VILLCODE", relationship = "one-to-one")
selected_store <- stores |> filter(Store_CD == "BT")
stopifnot(nrow(Trade_area) == nrow(village), !anyNA(Trade_area$p_ij))
bt_breaks <- unique(as.numeric(quantile(Trade_area$p_ij, seq(0, 1, 0.1))))
bt_labels <- paste(trimws(formatC(head(bt_breaks, -1), format = "g", digits = 4)),
                   "to", trimws(formatC(tail(bt_breaks, -1), format = "g", digits = 4)))
tm_shape(village_raw) + tm_polygons(fill = "grey85", col = "grey60") +
  tm_shape(Trade_area) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "p_ij", col = "grey50", lwd = 0.4,
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(breaks = bt_breaks, labels = bt_labels,
                                    interval.closure = "right",
                                    values = "brewer.blues", label.na = FALSE),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "BT probability",
                            position = tm_pos_out("right", "center"))
  ) +
  tm_shape(selected_store) + tm_dots(size = 0.3, fill = "red", col = "black") +
  tm_title("Distribution of patronage probability: store BT") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2, position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom")) +
  tm_scalebar(position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom")) + tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)
```

BT's probabilities range from `r signif(min(Trade_area$p_ij), 3)` to `r signif(max(Trade_area$p_ij), 3)`. A high probability here means BT has a relatively strong position within the specified choice set; it is not a measured share of observed visits.

```{r}
#| label: bt-leading-villages

kable(Trade_area |> st_drop_geometry() |>
        select(VILLCODE, VILLENG, P_CNT, p_ij) |>
        arrange(desc(p_ij)) |> head(5), digits = 4,
      col.names = c("Village code", "Village", "Population", "BT probability"),
      caption = "The five villages with the largest BT probabilities")
```

## Classroom extension: dominant-store trade areas

The photographs show `huff_share_wider`, `huff_TA`, `huff_TA_tidied` and a map of `village_TA` coloured by `TA`. They do not show the preceding assignment code. I interpret the displayed categories as the store with the highest probability in each village and make that rule explicit.

### Deriving TA and joining it to the polygons

The wide table contains one row per village and one named probability column per store. The supplied `storeCD.csv` confirms the same 28 store codes. Its `Capacity = 50` field is not substituted for the chapter's `Store_size = 100` attractiveness assumption. The helper uses real store-code column names, not a column number or a `fid` that could be mistaken for a store code. It verifies the probabilities, records the runner-up and gap, and reports ties within a numerical tolerance of `1e-12`. A tie is assigned to the first store code in lexical order solely to make the categorical display reproducible.

```{r}
#| label: derive-dominant-trade-areas

huff_share_wider <- huff_share |>
  select(VILLCODE, Store_CD, p_ij) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Store_CD, values_from = p_ij) |>
  select(VILLCODE, all_of(sort(stores$Store_CD)))
huff_TA <- dominant_trade_areas(huff_share_wider, stores$Store_CD)
huff_TA_tidied <- huff_TA |>
  mutate(TA = factor(TA, levels = sort(stores$Store_CD)))
village_TA <- village |>
  left_join(huff_TA_tidied, by = "VILLCODE", relationship = "one-to-one")
stopifnot(
  nrow(village_TA) == nrow(village), !anyNA(village_TA$TA),
  !anyDuplicated(village_TA$VILLCODE),
  all(as.character(village_TA$TA) %in% stores$Store_CD)
)
nearest_check <- huff_share |>
  group_by(VILLCODE) |>
  summarise(Nearest = min(distance), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(huff_TA |> select(VILLCODE, TA), by = "VILLCODE") |>
  left_join(huff_share |> select(VILLCODE, Store_CD, distance),
            by = join_by(VILLCODE, TA == Store_CD))
stopifnot(all(abs(nearest_check$distance - nearest_check$Nearest) < 1e-6))
```

All else being equal, the highest-probability store is also the nearest one under these equal-attractiveness assumptions. The additional distance check verifies that consequence rather than treating the categorical result as a separate model.

### Mapping TA using the classroom layout

This follows the visible plotting sequence: `tm_shape(village_TA)`, categorical `tm_polygons(fill = "TA")`, title, frame, village borders, eight-point compass, scale bar and grid. I set the border's colour transparency explicitly with `col_alpha`, rather than applying a fill setting to a line layer. The categorical legend sits outside the map so it cannot cover villages.

```{r}
#| label: map-store-trade-areas
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 12
#| fig-cap: "Dominant-store trade areas; TA is the highest-probability store code, not an exclusive customer boundary"

store_colours <- setNames(hcl.colors(nrow(stores), palette = "Dynamic"), stores$Store_CD)
tm_shape(village_raw) + tm_polygons(fill = "grey85", col = "grey65") +
  tm_shape(village_TA) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "TA", col = "grey35", lwd = 0.5,
    fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = store_colours, label.na = FALSE),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "TA", text.size = 0.65,
                            position = tm_pos_out("right", "center"))
  ) +
  tm_title("Trade Areas of stores") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey30", col_alpha = 0.5, lwd = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2, position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom")) +
  tm_scalebar(position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom")) + tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)
```

There are `r sum(huff_TA$Tied_stores > 1)` tied villages under the stated tolerance. The median gap between the leading two stores is `r round(median(huff_TA$Probability_gap), 3)`. A small gap means that a sharp colour boundary can hide a close competition; the original probabilities should be consulted alongside this summary map.

## Population-weighted allocations and recorded sales

TG ranks first in `r sum(huff_TA$TA == "TG")` villages, the largest count in this classification, while BT ranks first in `r sum(huff_TA$TA == "BT")`. These counts are not the store-level demand ranking: villages differ in population, and the Huff allocation also includes fractional demand from villages where another store ranks first. A large coloured area should therefore not be read as a large observed customer base.

Following the chapter, `shares.total()` multiplies each village's probability by its population and sums over villages for each store. Its result, $E_j=\sum_iP_i p_{ij}$, is an allocated population under the model. Because `P_CNT` counts residents, the result is not a monetary sales estimate. Converting it to currency would require assumptions about spending and participation that these files do not establish.

```{r}
#| label: population-allocations

huff_share_pp <- huff_share |>
  left_join(st_drop_geometry(village) |> select(VILLCODE, P_CNT),
            by = "VILLCODE", relationship = "many-to-one")
stopifnot(!anyNA(huff_share_pp$P_CNT))
huff_total <- shares.total(
  huff_share_pp, "VILLCODE", "Store_CD", "p_ij", "P_CNT"
)
direct_totals <- huff_share_pp |>
  group_by(Store_CD) |>
  summarise(Direct = sum(P_CNT * p_ij), .groups = "drop")
store_sales_est <- stores |>
  left_join(huff_total, by = join_by(Store_CD == suppliers_single),
            relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  left_join(direct_totals, by = "Store_CD", relationship = "one-to-one")
stopifnot(
  !anyNA(store_sales_est$sum_E_j),
  max(abs(store_sales_est$sum_E_j - store_sales_est$Direct)) < 1e-6,
  abs(sum(store_sales_est$sum_E_j) - sum(village$P_CNT)) < 1e-6
)
ta_summary <- village_TA |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(TA, .drop = FALSE) |>
  summarise(Dominant_villages = n(), Dominant_population = sum(P_CNT),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(Store_CD = as.character(TA)) |>
  select(-TA)
store_sales_nongeom <- store_sales_est |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  left_join(ta_summary, by = "Store_CD", relationship = "one-to-one")
kable(store_sales_nongeom |>
        select(Store_CD, Dominant_villages, Dominant_population, sum_E_j, Total_Sales) |>
        arrange(desc(sum_E_j)), digits = 1,
      format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
      col.names = c("Store", "Dominant villages", "Population in TA",
                    "Probability-weighted population", "Recorded sales amount"))
```

The weighted allocations sum to `r fmt(round(sum(store_sales_est$sum_E_j)))`, matching the included population. Dominant-area population is a different quantity: it assigns each village wholly to one store, whereas the Huff allocation distributes its population fractionally across the choice set.

```{r}
#| label: compare-with-recorded-sales
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Descriptive association between population-weighted allocations and recorded sales amounts"

ggscatterstats(
  store_sales_nongeom, x = sum_E_j, y = Total_Sales,
  type = "parametric", bf.message = FALSE, label.var = Store_CD,
  xlab = "Probability-weighted population (resident-equivalents)",
  ylab = "Recorded sales amount (source units)",
  title = "Modelled store allocations and recorded sales"
)
association <- tibble(
  Pearson_r = cor(store_sales_nongeom$sum_E_j, store_sales_nongeom$Total_Sales),
  Spearman_rho = cor(store_sales_nongeom$sum_E_j, store_sales_nongeom$Total_Sales,
                     method = "spearman")
)
kable(association, digits = 3)
```

Pearson's correlation describes linear association, while Spearman's describes agreement in ranking. Neither turns resident-equivalents into currency or establishes out-of-sample forecasting accuracy. The stores share a spatial market, so the statistical test shown on the chart should not be treated as proof of independent observations or a causal relationship.

## Interpretation and limitations

BT has the largest population-weighted allocation, at `r fmt(round(store_sales_nongeom$sum_E_j[store_sales_nongeom$Store_CD == "BT"]))` resident-equivalents, or `r round(100 * store_sales_nongeom$share_j[store_sales_nongeom$Store_CD == "BT"], 2)`% of included demand. FH has the largest recorded sales amount. Those different leaders show why the equal-attractiveness distance model should not be presented as a fitted revenue model.

The Pearson correlation is `r round(association$Pearson_r, 3)` and Spearman's rank correlation is `r round(association$Spearman_rho, 3)`. Both indicate a moderate positive association in this 28-store comparison, with substantial differences remaining between allocations and recorded sales. This is evidence of some agreement in the spatial-demand pattern, not proof of accurate individual-store sales predictions.

The BT map answers a store-specific probability question. The `TA` map answers which store ranks first in each village. The gap and tie fields help distinguish a clear lead from a nearly equal contest, which a categorical colour alone cannot show.

This is a closed choice set: each included village's probabilities sum to one across the supplied stores. Other brands, stores outside the study area, online orders and non-purchase are absent. Equal attractiveness omits differences in size, price and service. One representative point cannot describe all households within a village, and straight-line distance omits road layouts, congestion and travel mode.

The population is from 2019, and the sales period must be checked against the supplied file documentation before making a time-consistent comparison. Unmatched villages are excluded, not treated as empty. This analysis supports interpretation of a teaching scenario; it is not a verified current revenue forecast or a recommendation to invest in a particular site.

## Reproducibility

The source preserves the chapter's `st_read()`, explicit `left_join()`, `st_point_on_surface()`, `st_distance()`, `huff.shares()` and `shares.total()` workflow. The classroom extension adds the named wide probability matrix, `huff_TA`, `huff_TA_tidied`, `village_TA` and categorical `TA` map. The assignment helper is tested separately with synthetic unit fixtures; the fixtures are not used as study data.

```{r}
#| label: save-results
#| include: false

write_csv(input_counts, "results/input-counts.csv")
write_csv(excluded_villages, "results/excluded-villages.csv")
write_csv(unmatched_population, "results/unmatched-population.csv")
write_csv(sales_without_location, "results/sales-without-location.csv")
write_csv(huff_share |> select(VILLCODE, Store_CD, distance, p_ij),
          "results/huff-probabilities.csv")
write_csv(huff_share_wider, "results/huff-share-wide.csv")
write_csv(huff_TA, "results/dominant-store-trade-areas.csv")
write_csv(store_sales_nongeom, "results/store-allocations.csv")
write_csv(probability_checks, "results/probability-checks.csv")
write_csv(association, "results/sales-association.csv")
write_csv(tibble(File = required_files,
                 MD5 = unname(tools::md5sum(required_files))),
          "results/input-checksums.csv")
writeLines(trimws(capture.output(sessionInfo()), which = "right"),
           "results/session-info.txt")
```
